learn.hook: In 1820 a compass needle twitched near a wire carrying current — and electricity and magnetism turned out to be best friends!
points: A compass needle is a small bar magnet; its north-seeking end is its north pole. The space around a magnet where its force can be detected is its magnetic field — it has both strength and direction.

Magnetic field lines come out of the north pole and go into the south pole outside the magnet, and run from south to north inside it, so they are closed curves. Where lines are crowded the field is stronger. Two field lines never cross, because a compass cannot point in two directions at one place.
Hans Christian Oersted found in 1820 that a compass needle deflects near a wire carrying current — a current produces a magnetic field.

Around a straight current-carrying wire, field lines are concentric circles. Right-hand thumb rule: hold the wire in your right hand with the thumb along the current; your curled fingers show the direction of the field. The field is stronger for a larger current and weaker farther from the wire.

For a circular loop, the circles near the wire grow larger towards the centre, where the lines look nearly straight. The field of a coil increases with the number of turns, since the fields of the turns add up.

example.q: Think it through: current flows vertically upward in a straight wire passing through a horizontal card. Which way do the field lines circle when seen from above?
steps: Point your right thumb upward along the current.
Your fingers curl around the wire.
Seen from above, the curl is anticlockwise.

learn.reallife: When you sprinkle iron filings on paper over a bar magnet in the school lab, they line up along the field lines, making the invisible field visible.

games.title: Field line facts
items: Magnetic field lines outside a magnet go from the north pole to the south pole.
Inside the magnet they go from south to north, making closed loops.
Two magnetic field lines can cross each other.
At a crossing a compass would point two ways at once, which is impossible.
Field lines are crowded where the magnetic field is strong.
The closeness of lines shows the strength of the field.
The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles.
The circles are centred on the wire.
Increasing the current in a wire weakens its magnetic field.
A larger current gives a stronger field.
A coil with more turns produces a stronger magnetic field at its centre for the same current.
The fields due to each turn add up.

games.title: Match the situation to the field pattern
pairs: Lines from N to S outside, S to N inside

quiz.q: Who discovered that an electric current deflects a nearby compass needle?
quiz.explain: Oersted observed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.
quiz.mistake: Credits a famous scientist from another topic

quiz.q: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect?
options: Because they are drawn far apart
Because a compass at the crossing would point in two directions at once
Because the field is zero there
quiz.explain: The field has only one direction at any point, so lines cannot cross.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a drawing convention only

quiz.q: Inside a bar magnet, the field lines run —
quiz.explain: Field lines are closed curves: N → S outside and S → N inside.
quiz.mistake: Applies the outside direction inside too

quiz.q: What is the pattern of the magnetic field around a straight wire carrying current?
options: Lines from one end to the other
Concentric circles centred on the wire
quiz.explain: The field lines form circles around the wire in planes perpendicular to it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the straight wire with a solenoid

quiz.q: What happens to the magnetic field at a point near a straight wire if the current is increased?
quiz.explain: The field strength is directly related to the current.
quiz.mistake: Thinks current direction and magnitude effects are the same

quiz.q: The right-hand thumb rule gives the —
options: Direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
Direction of force on a conductor
quiz.explain: With the thumb along the current, curled fingers show the field's direction.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Fleming's left-hand rule

quiz.q: A coil of 50 turns is replaced by one of 100 turns carrying the same current. The field at its centre —
quiz.explain: Each turn adds its field, so doubling the turns about doubles the field.
quiz.mistake: Thinks number of turns does not matter

quiz.q: The magnetic field near a current-carrying straight wire is weaker —
options: Only when the current is large
quiz.explain: The field decreases as the distance from the wire increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field is uniform everywhere

teach.ask: Gappu perches on a wire: 'A compass needle wiggled when current flowed! Does a wire become a magnet?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A current makes a magnetic field in circles around the wire — and my right thumb tells me which way!
teach.nudge: Good! What shape does the field around a straight wire have?

topics.title: Solenoid, electromagnet and force on a conductor

learn.hook: Wrap wire around an iron nail, connect a cell, and pick up pins — you just built a magnet you can switch off!
points: A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. Its field pattern is like a bar magnet's: one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
Inside a solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform there.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. It is a strong magnet only while current flows, and its strength can be increased with more current or more turns.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The force is greatest when the current is perpendicular to the field, and reversing the current or the field reverses the force.

Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. Forefinger → field, middle finger → current, thumb → direction of motion (force). Loudspeakers and measuring instruments use this force.

example.q: Think it through: a wire carries current from left to right across a magnetic field pointing into the page. Which way is the force?
steps: Thumb then points upward, towards the top of the page.
example.answer: The force is upward (towards the top of the page).

learn.reallife: Cranes in scrap yards use huge electromagnets to lift heavy iron pieces, then simply switch off the current to drop them.

games.title: Make an electromagnet
items: Take an iron nail as the soft iron core
Wind insulated copper wire closely around it
Connect the ends of the wire to a cell through a switch
Switch on the current
Bring pins near — they get attracted

quiz.q: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is —
quiz.explain: Inside a solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, showing a uniform field.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field inside is like that around a straight wire

quiz.q: Which material is best for the core of an electromagnet?
quiz.explain: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetised when current flows and loses magnetism when it stops.
quiz.mistake: Thinks copper, a good conductor, makes the best core

quiz.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the forefinger shows the direction of —
quiz.explain: Forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force or motion.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the fingers

quiz.q: When is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field the greatest?
options: When the current is parallel to the field
When the current is perpendicular to the field
quiz.explain: The force is maximum when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the force is largest when current is along the field

quiz.q: What happens to the force on a conductor if the direction of current is reversed?
quiz.explain: Reversing either the current or the field reverses the direction of the force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the field affects the force

quiz.q: The field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that of —
quiz.explain: One end of the solenoid acts as a north pole, the other as a south pole, just like a bar magnet.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a solenoid with a single wire

quiz.q: Which change makes an electromagnet stronger?
quiz.explain: More current or more turns gives a stronger magnetic field.
quiz.mistake: Thinks removing the core strengthens it

quiz.q: A scientist who suggested that a magnet also experiences an equal and opposite force from a current-carrying conductor was —
quiz.explain: Ampère suggested that since a current exerts a force on a magnet, the magnet must exert an equal and opposite force on the conductor.
quiz.mistake: Links the idea with Ohm because both studied electricity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can a coil of wire become a magnet only when I switch it on? And why does a wire jump in a magnet?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A coil carrying current is a solenoid; add soft iron and it's an electromagnet — and Fleming's left hand shows the force!
teach.nudge: Good! What must be placed inside the coil to make a strong electromagnet?

learn.hook: Behind every switchboard at home is a careful plan of three colour-coded wires that keep you safe!
points: Direct current (DC), from cells, flows in one direction. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction periodically. In India, AC has a frequency of 50 Hz — it changes direction every 1/100 second.
An advantage of AC over DC: electric power can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy.

Mains supply comes through a live wire (red insulation) and a neutral wire (black insulation); the potential difference between them in India is 220 V. The earth wire (green insulation) connects to a metal plate deep in the earth.

The earth wire is attached to metal bodies of appliances like irons, toasters and refrigerators. If the live wire touches the body, current flows safely to earth through this low-resistance path, so the user does not get a severe shock.

Homes have a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances (geysers, air coolers) and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans. Appliances are connected in parallel, each with its own switch. A fuse protects against short-circuiting (live and neutral wires touching) and overloading (too many appliances on one socket, or a sudden rise in supply voltage).

example.q: Think it through: why is an electric iron with a metal body connected with a three-pin plug?
steps: The third pin connects the metal body to the earth wire.
If current leaks to the metal body, the earth wire gives it a low-resistance path to the ground.
So the body stays at the earth's potential and the user is protected from a severe shock.
example.answer: The third (earth) pin safely carries any leaking current to the ground.

learn.reallife: Never plug a heater, an iron and a kettle into one extension board together — that can overload the circuit and is a common cause of electrical fires.

games.title: Which wire?
items: Red insulation
Black insulation
Green insulation
Connected to a metal plate buried deep in the ground
At 220 V relative to neutral
Attached to the metal body of an appliance
Completes the circuit back to the supply

items.q: Circuit rating for bulbs and fans (A)?
Live and neutral touching is called?

quiz.q: What is the frequency of AC supply in India, in hertz?
quiz.explain: Indian mains AC has a frequency of 50 Hz.
quiz.mistake: Confuses frequency with voltage

quiz.q: What is the potential difference between the live and neutral wires in Indian homes, in volts?
quiz.explain: In India the mains supply is at 220 V.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up voltage with frequency or current rating

quiz.q: What colour is the insulation of the earth wire?
quiz.explain: Live is red, neutral is black and earth is green.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the colour code

quiz.q: Why is the earth wire connected to the metal body of an appliance?
options: To provide a low-resistance path for leaking current, preventing a severe shock
quiz.explain: Any leakage current flows to earth instead of through the person touching the appliance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks earthing is needed for the appliance to work

quiz.q: What is short-circuiting?
options: When too few appliances are used
When the fuse is rated 15 A
When the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact
quiz.explain: Direct contact lowers resistance sharply, so the current rises abruptly and the fuse should blow.
quiz.mistake: Confuses short-circuit with overloading

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of AC over DC?
options: AC always flows in one direction
AC can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy
quiz.explain: That is why power stations send AC to our homes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AC is safer to touch

quiz.q: Which appliance should be on the 15 A circuit?
quiz.explain: High-power appliances like geysers draw large currents and use the 15 A circuit.
quiz.mistake: Does not link high power with high current

quiz.q: Overloading of a household circuit can happen when —
options: Too many appliances are connected to a single socket
quiz.explain: Too many appliances draw too much current; an accidental rise in supply voltage can also overload a circuit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks overloading is caused by wire colours

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do some plugs have three pins? What is that extra one for?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The third pin is the earth — it gives leaking current a low-resistance path to the ground, so no shock!
teach.nudge: Good! Where does the leaking current go through the earth wire, and how does that protect us?
